snapshot.title: SSC Reasoning: Seating & Puzzles
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC Reasoning Hook: Inside circle: Right: Anti, Left: Clock. Linear: Start at ends. Opposites: n/2. Use pencil and circles.

quick_notes.title: Circular Arrangement
quick_notes.detail: 1. Facing Inside : Clockwise is Left, Anti-clockwise is Right. 2. Facing Outside : Clockwise is Right, Anti-clockwise is Left.
quick_notes.explanation: In a circular arrangement, people or objects are placed around a circle, and their direction matters. If everyone is facing the center of the circle, then moving clockwise means you are turning to your left, and moving anti-clockwise means you are turning to your right. If everyone is facing outward away from the center, then moving clockwise means you are turning to your right, and moving anti-clockwise means you are turning to your left. To solve problems, first check whether the people are facing inside or outside, then use these rules to figure out who is sitting next to whom. For example, if three people A, B, and C sit in a circle facing the center, and you go clockwise from A, you will reach B on A's left side.

quick_notes.title: Linear Arrangement
quick_notes.detail: Facing North: Left is towards the left of the page, Right is towards the right. Facing South : Reverse.
quick_notes.explanation: In linear arrangement problems, you imagine people sitting in a straight line and facing a specific direction, either north or south. When they face north, their left side is the same as the left side of the page you draw, and their right side is the same as the right side of the page

quick_notes.title: Important Terms
quick_notes.detail: "Immediate Left" (No one in between). "Between" (Exactly in middle). "Opposite" (Facing across the center).
quick_notes.explanation: Immediate Left means the person who is directly to your left with no other person in between you and that person. Between means a person who is exactly in the middle of two other people, with one person on each side of them. Opposite means two people who are facing each other across a center point, such as across a table or a circle. For example, in a row of seats, the person sitting immediately left of you has no one sitting between you and them. In a line of three people, the second person is between the first and third. In a circular arrangement, the person directly across from you is your opposite.

quick_notes.title: Constraint Solving
quick_notes.detail: Start with a definite clue (e.g., A sits at the end). Use secondary clues to fill the gaps.
quick_notes.explanation: Constraint solving is a way to figure out a puzzle where you have to arrange items, like people in a row, based on rules. A definite clue is a rule that gives you a fixed spot for something, for example, a rule that says "A sits at the end" means A is placed at the very first or very last position in the row. Secondary clues are rules that do not give a fixed spot but tell you how items relate to each other, like "B is two places to the left of C," which means you can find B and C's positions only after you have placed A. To solve the puzzle, you start by putting the definite clue's item, like A, in its exact spot, and then you use the secondary clues one by one to figure out where the other items go, filling in the empty spaces until the whole arrangement is complete.

quick_notes.title: Ordering Puzzle
quick_notes.detail: Arranging by height, marks, or age. (e.g., A > B but shorter than C).
quick_notes.explanation: In an ordering puzzle, you are given statements about how people or objects compare to each other based on a single quality, such as height, test scores, or age. For example, a statement might say "A is taller than B but shorter than C," which means A is in the middle, B is the shortest, and C is the tallest. To solve it, you arrange everyone in a straight line from lowest to highest or highest to lowest, using each clue to place one person relative to the others. If you see "A is taller than B," write A above or to the right of B in your line. Always check that your final order does not break any clue, and remember that words like "shorter" mean lower height, while "marks" are scores, so "higher marks" means a better score.
